subject: data-science
question: Does a training accuracy of 1.0 show the model will perform well on new customers?

artifact.code:
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier()          # no depth limit
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(tree.score(X_train, y_train))      # 1.0

ai_claim: Yes. The model classifies every training example correctly, so it has learned the pattern and will perform well on new data.

ai_solution.text: The model was trained on X_train.
It scores 100% on the same data.
Perfect accuracy means it has learned the pattern.
So it will perform well on new customers.

failure.misconception: Judging a model on the data it was trained on
failure.explanation: An unrestricted decision tree can memorise the training set, reaching 100% by fitting noise. Training accuracy says nothing about new data. Evaluate on a held-out test set (or with cross-validation); a large gap between training and test accuracy signals overfitting.
failure.why_convincing: 100% sounds like the best possible result.

canonical_solution: No: training accuracy cannot measure generalisation, and an unlimited tree memorises. Evaluate on held-out data.

valid_evidence.summary: tree.score(X_test, y_test) is much lower than 1.0, e.g. 0.71.
The tree has no depth limit, so it can grow a leaf for every training example.

counterexamples: A model that memorised the training set fails on new customers.

hints.text: Ask what data the score was computed on.
Step 3 treats training accuracy as learning.
Generalisation is measured on data the model has not seen.
Score the model on X_test.
Step 3 is wrong: perfect training accuracy often means memorisation. Evaluate on held-out data.

repair: Hold out a test set (or use cross-validation) and limit tree depth.
debrief: Never report a model's score on its own training data. The held-out score is the only estimate of how it will do in use.

subject: data-science
question: Are the predictions valid churn probabilities between 0 and 1?

artifact.code:
# churned is 0 or 1
reg = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
prob = reg.predict(X_new)      # used as 'probability of churn'

ai_claim: Yes. The target is 0 or 1, so the regression's predictions lie between 0 and 1 and can be read as probabilities.

ai_solution.text: The target takes values 0 and 1.
Linear regression fits the target.
So its predictions lie between 0 and 1.
They are churn probabilities.

failure.explanation: A linear model's output is unbounded: extreme feature values give predictions like -0.3 or 1.4, which are not probabilities. The straight line also fits the 0/1 target poorly. Use logistic regression (or another classifier) and predict_proba for probabilities.
failure.why_convincing: On typical customers the predictions do fall between 0 and 1.

canonical_solution: No: linear regression predictions can fall outside [0, 1]. Use LogisticRegression and predict_proba.

valid_evidence.summary: For a customer with extreme feature values, reg.predict returns 1.4.
Some predictions on X_new are negative.

hints.text: Ask what bounds a linear model's output.
Step 3 assumes the output stays within the target's range.
Linear predictions are unbounded; logistic regression maps to (0, 1).
Predict for a customer with extreme values.
Step 3 is wrong: predictions can be below 0 or above 1. Use logistic regression.

debrief: Match the model to the target: classifiers for categories, regressors for quantities. Probabilities need a model that produces them.

subject: data-science
question: Is customer A, who is almost the same age as the query customer, chosen as the query's nearest neighbour?
ai_claim: Yes. A differs from the query by just 1 year of age, while B differs by 29 years, so A is the nearest neighbour.

ai_solution.text: A is 30 and the query is 31: 1 year apart.
B is 60: 29 years apart.
Incomes are similar for all three.
So A is the nearest neighbour.

failure.misconception: Assuming features contribute equally to distance
failure.explanation: Euclidean distance uses raw units. Income differs by Rs 60,000 from A and Rs 50,000 from B, which swamps any age difference: the distance to A is about 60,000 and to B about 50,000. B is chosen. Standardise features (StandardScaler in a pipeline) before distance-based models.
failure.why_convincing: People compare customers by noticing that age differs a lot, but the metric does not.

canonical_solution: No: the income gaps (60,000 vs 50,000) dominate, so B is nearest. Scale the features first.

valid_evidence.summary: dist(query, A) = sqrt(1^2 + 60000^2) = about 60,000; dist(query, B) = sqrt(29^2 + 50000^2) = about 50,000
knn.kneighbors on the query returns B.

counterexamples: Age barely affects the distance at all.

hints.text: Compute the Euclidean distances with the raw values.
Step 3 dismisses the income differences.
Features on large scales dominate distance unless standardised.
Compare the income gaps with the age gaps.
Step 3 is wrong: income differences dominate, so B is nearest. Standardise the features.

debrief: Distance-based models (k-NN, k-means, SVMs with RBF kernels) are sensitive to units. Scale features, inside a pipeline fitted on training data only.

subject: data-science
subtopic: The same customer in train and test
question: Is 0.97 a reliable estimate of how well the model predicts default for new customers?

artifact.code:
# transactions: many rows per customer; label = customer later defaulted
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(transactions_X, transactions_y, test_size=0.2)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.score(X_test, y_test))     # 0.97

ai_claim: Yes. The test set was held out from training, so 0.97 is an unbiased estimate of performance on new customers.

ai_solution.text: 20% of rows were held out as a test set.
The model never saw those rows during training.
Unseen rows represent new data.
So 0.97 is reliable for new customers.

failure.misconception: Splitting by row when rows share an entity
failure.explanation: The split is by transaction, so most test customers also have transactions in the training set. The model can recognise customers (and their label) rather than learn general signals, inflating the score. New customers have no rows in training. Split by customer with GroupShuffleSplit or GroupKFold.
failure.why_convincing: The test rows are genuinely unseen as rows.

canonical_solution: No: the same customers appear on both sides of a row-level split. Split by customer (GroupKFold) for an honest estimate.

valid_evidence.summary: About 95% of customers in X_test also have rows in X_train.
With GroupShuffleSplit by customer_id, the test score drops to 0.78.

counterexamples: A customer's other transactions reveal their label to the model.

hints.text: Ask whether test customers also appear in training.
Step 3 equates unseen rows with unseen customers.
When rows are grouped by an entity, split by the entity.
Count customers present in both sets.
Step 3 is wrong: customers overlap. Split by customer.

debrief: The test set must mimic the deployment situation. If the model will see new customers, the test set must contain only customers it has never seen.

subject: data-science
question: Is the AI right that max_depth = 6 is the best choice here, and that deeper trees overfit?
ai_claim: Yes. Validation accuracy peaks at depth 6 (0.82). Beyond it, training accuracy keeps rising while validation accuracy falls - the signature of overfitting. Shallower trees underfit.

ai_solution.text: Depth 2 scores 0.74 on training and 0.73 on validation: underfitting.
Validation accuracy rises to its maximum, 0.82, at depth 6.
At depth 10 and unlimited depth, training accuracy rises to 0.95 and 1.00 while validation falls to 0.78 and 0.71.
So depth 6 balances bias and variance.

canonical_solution: Correct. Choose hyperparameters by validation performance; the widening train-validation gap beyond depth 6 indicates overfitting.

valid_evidence.summary: Validation accuracy peaks at 0.82 at depth 6.
Train-validation gap: 0.04 at depth 6, 0.29 with no limit.

hints.text: Find where validation accuracy is highest.
Step 3 compares training and validation trends.
Overfitting shows as rising training scores with falling validation scores.
Compute the gap at each depth.
This solution is correct. Depth 6 maximises validation accuracy; deeper trees overfit. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: The bias-variance trade-off is visible in any validation curve. Pick the complexity that maximises validation performance - then confirm on a final test set.
